Property documentation translation for real estate and lettings

June 5, 2019
Property Translation | Translation | Travel and Tourism

Property translation covers far more than a single contract. Sale agreements, leases, title deeds, surveys and mortgage paperwork all pass between buyers, landlords, agents, lenders and solicitors, and any of them may read a different language from the one on the page.

A mistranslated clause can delay a completion, cost a deal or leave a tenant bound by terms they never understood. If you run an estate agency, a lettings business or a holiday let portfolio in the UK, a professional real estate translation service protects both your clients and your reputation.

Which property documents need translating?

The documents you translate depend on who is buying, renting or investing and where they live. These are the ones agents and landlords ask for most often:

  • Sale and purchase agreements, including schedules and special conditions
  • Tenancy agreements, lease agreements and rental contracts
  • Title deeds, title registers and plans
  • Mortgage offers, valuation reports and surveys
  • Energy performance certificates, inventories and management agreements
  • Powers of attorney and company documents used to buy through an overseas entity

Each of these mixes legal wording, figures and local conventions. That combination is why property documents reward a translator who knows the sector.

Why property contracts are not a job for machine translation

Terms such as freehold, leasehold, ground rent, tenants in common and exchange of contracts belong to English and Welsh property law. Many legal systems have no exact equivalent, so a word-for-word rendering can describe a right that does not exist in the buyer's country.

Free online tools also struggle with long sentences, defined terms that recur across a contract and the numbers that matter most, such as dates, deposits and notice periods. A single slip in a rent review clause or a completion date can change what each party has agreed to. Machine output is fine for getting the gist of a brochure, but it cannot take responsibility for a contract.

Do you need a certified translation of property documents?

It depends on who receives the translation. Conveyancing solicitors, lenders, HM Land Registry, overseas notaries and local authorities each set their own rules, so ask the receiving party what it accepts before you order.

HM Land Registry, for example, does not translate register entries and states that arranging a translation is the responsibility of the customer or their solicitor. A certified translation carries a signed statement from the translator or agency confirming that it is a complete and accurate rendering of the original. BeTranslated's document translation services cover certified options, and the legal translation team handles contracts and deeds.

How to get a property agreement or lease translated

A clear process keeps a transaction moving. A well-run property translation project follows these steps:

  1. Send the full document, including annexes, schedules and plans, so the translator sees every defined term.
  2. Tell your project manager who will read the translation, in which country and for what purpose.
  3. Agree key terminology, such as how freehold and leasehold should be rendered, before translation starts.
  4. A native translator with property and legal experience produces the translation, and it is checked before it reaches you.
  5. You receive the final file in the same layout as the original, with certification if you asked for it.

Ask about confidentiality before you send anything, because property files often contain personal and financial details. Tell the project manager if your files are scanned PDFs or Word documents so the finished translation can follow the original layout.

Translating property listings, brochures and websites

Overseas buyers and tenants usually start with a listing, not a contract. Property descriptions, floor plan notes, virtual tour scripts and neighbourhood guides need to read naturally to a buyer in Madrid, Paris or Seoul, not like a translation.

Localisation goes further than translation. It adapts measurements, currencies, tenure terms and search keywords so your pages reach people searching in their own language. If you let holiday homes or serviced apartments, BeTranslated's tourism translation and website translation services can adapt your listings for each market.

What to look for in a property translation partner

Choose a partner who can show relevant experience and explain how they check their work. Four questions are worth asking:

  • Do your translators work into their native language and have legal or property experience?
  • Can you provide a certified translation if your solicitor or lender requires one?
  • Is the translation checked by a second linguist before delivery?
  • How do you keep your documents confidential?

BeTranslated works with native linguists in many languages, including Spanish, French, German and Korean. Tell the team about your property documents and request a free, no-obligation quote.

Frequently asked questions

How much does property translation cost?

The price depends on word count, language pair, how technical the document is and whether you need certification. Send your file to get a quote before any work begins, and see the translation rates page for an overview.

Can I use Google Translate for a tenancy agreement?

You can use it to get a rough idea of what a document says. You should not rely on it for a signed agreement, because legal terms, dates and amounts need a human translator who takes responsibility for the result.

Does my solicitor need a certified translation?

Ask your solicitor or the receiving organisation what they accept. Lenders, registries and overseas notaries each have their own requirements, and a certified translation is often the safest choice for formal transactions.

Can you translate a property deed or title register?

Yes. Deeds and registers contain formal wording, plan references and legal descriptions, so they go to a linguist with legal experience. Send the full document including any plans so the translator can see the context.

Which languages do you translate property documents into?

BeTranslated covers the main languages used by overseas buyers and tenants. Check the languages page for the full list, and ask if your language pair is not shown.
